title: ADT R27A-BK3 U.2 to PCIe Adapter Review
gist: ServeTheHome reviews the ADT R27A-BK3, an inexpensive adapter that puts a U.2 (SFF-8639) NVMe SSD in a PCIe Gen5 x4 slot, with a metal shell and a PWM blower fan. In 20-minute sustained tests, a Gen3 Samsung drive held 2,179 MB/s (3.2% off peak) and a Gen5 Solidigm D7-PS1010 held 7,838 MB/s (1.4% off peak). Neither throttled, unlike the EDSFF version of the adapter in earlier testing.

themes.theme: R27A-BK3 design: Gen5 x4 slot to U.2 SFF-8639

insights.claim: The ADT R27A-BK3 is a low-cost adapter that lets a U.2 NVMe SSD be installed in a system with only standard PCIe slots. It uses a PCIe Gen5 x4 edge connector and an SFF-8639 drive connector, and it encloses the full-length drive in a metal shell with a 4-pin PWM blower fan.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Cheap retrofit adapters make it easier to put used or enterprise U.2 drives into workstations and homelab machines that have no U.2 backplane.
insights.quote: The bottom edge carries a PCIe Gen5 x4 gold-finger connector.
insights.locator: The bottom edge carries a PCIe Gen5 x4 gold-finger connector

insights.claim: ADT sells the adapter family in several versions: a Gen4 version, a Gen5 version, and an EDSFF variant that uses an SFF-TA-1002 connector for E1.S/E3.S drives under a different model number. The R27A-BK3 works only with U.2 SFF-8639 drives, so buyers need to match both the PCIe generation and the drive form factor.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: The adapter models are split by connector and generation, so buying the wrong SKU is a real risk for anyone purchasing them in bulk.
insights.locator: Just make sure you buy the correct version

insights.claim: In a 20-minute test in the R27A-BK3, a Samsung MZQLB7T6HMLA-00007 (7.68TB, PCIe Gen3 x4) peaked at 2,252 MB/s and sustained 2,179 MB/s, a drop of about 3.2%. The drive reached a peak temperature of 78 C, below its 86 C warning threshold.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Older Gen3 enterprise U.2 drives run at close to full speed in the adapter. That makes it a workable way to reuse them.
insights.quote: Temperature peaked at 78 C, staying well below the drive’s warning threshold of 86 C.
insights.locator: During a 20-minute run, the Samsung drive peaked

insights.claim: A Solidigm D7-PS1010 (7.68TB, PCIe Gen5 x4) in the R27A-BK3 peaked at 7,946 MB/s and sustained 7,838 MB/s over 20 minutes of 128K sequential writes, a drop of only 1.4%. Its temperature leveled off at 70 C, against a 77 C warning threshold.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: A cheap passive adapter can carry close to full Gen5 x4 bandwidth, so native U.2 backplanes are not strictly needed for high-throughput single-drive setups.
insights.quote: The performance drop from peak to sustained was minimal at just 1.4%.
insights.locator: The Solidigm drive achieved a peak throughput

themes.theme: Thermals: U.2 version versus EDSFF version

insights.claim: STH saw no sustained thermal throttling with either drive in the U.2 R27A-BK3, while the EDSFF version of the same adapter family did throttle in earlier testing. The enclosed shell and blower fan are what keep the U.2 drive cool.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: How well these cheap adapters cool the drive depends on the variant. The U.2 version looks more reliable than the EDSFF version for sustained workloads.
insights.quote: In our testing, we did not see the same thermal throttling behavior we saw with the EDSFF version of this adapter.

insights.claim: The reviewer cautions that the cooling is adequate for the drives tested, but users with hotter drives should check thermals in their own machine rather than assume the adapter will keep the drive within limits.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Anyone deploying hotter or higher-power Gen5 drives in this adapter should monitor drive temperatures. The test results do not guarantee the adapter's cooling headroom.
insights.locator: Neither drive exhibited sustained thermal throttling
